title: Active Brownian motion in a single-relaxation viscoelastic fluid
abstract: Active Brownian particles (ABPs) in viscoelastic (VE) media exhibit fascinating dynamical phenomena set by self-propulsion, thermal fluctuations, and fluid viscoelasticity. We extend our model, in which the Brownian dynamics within a slowly diffusing harmonic well emulates that in a single-relaxation VE fluid, to study active Brownian motion in such media. Consequently, the resultant dynamics is governed by the interplay of the characteristic timescales of the systems: the crossover and equilibration times of the VE fluid, $τ_k$ and $λ$, respectively, and the persistence time of the ABP, $τ_{\mathrm{R}}$. Following analytical predictions and simulations, we study two practically relevant regimes where the dynamics is dominated by the persistence of active motion and the elastic confinement of the VE fluid, with a phoretically active Pt-coated Janus colloid in a dynamic optical trap, and show quantitative agreement with the simulations. This approach provides a VE environment with tunable VE properties that remain unaffected by the strength of self-propulsion, allowing us to systematically investigate active Brownian motion in VE media in ways that are not otherwise possible with physical VE fluids.
summary: This work models Active Brownian Particles moving through a single-relaxation viscoelastic fluid, demonstrating that the resulting dynamics are dictated by the interplay between active self-propulsion and fluid memory effects. By analyzing the Mean Squared Displacement across different timescale orderings ($	au_R$, $	au_k$, $\lambda$), the authors provide a comprehensive theoretical framework validated by both simulation and experiment using an optical trap setup.
main_problem: The study investigates Active Brownian Motion (ABM) dynamics within viscoelastic (VE) media, focusing on how fluid memory effects alter particle movement compared to simple Newtonian solvents.
main_result: The Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) reveals distinct intermediate dynamic regimes—depending on the relative ordering of active persistence time ($	au_R$), VE equilibration time ($	au_k$), and relaxation time ($\lambda$)—validating the model against both simulation and experiment.
method: The authors combine analytical derivations for the MSD with numerical simulations, validating the theoretical framework using an experimental setup involving a Janus colloid in a dynamic optical trap.
model_or_system: The system models Active Brownian Particles (ABPs) moving in a single-relaxation viscoelastic fluid, mathematically described by combining contributions from active motion and harmonic/Maxwell-Voigt rheological elements. The experiment uses Pt-coated Janus colloids trapped optically to emulate the tunable VE environment.
key_observables: Mean Squared Displacement (MSD), which exhibits successive regimes including superdiffusive behavior, plateaus at characteristic timescales ($	au_k$ or $	au_R$), and long-time diffusive recovery.
important_parameters: The dynamics are governed by the interplay of three competing timescales: ABP persistence time ($	au_R$), VE equilibration time ($	au_k$), and VE relaxation time ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes linear viscoelasticity with a single relaxation time, and that the optical trap setup successfully emulates the required VE response without altering the medium due to activity.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows simulated MSDs for persistence-dominated ($	au_R < 	au_k < \lambda$) and confinement-dominated ($	au_k < 	au_R < \lambda$) regimes. Figure 4 presents experimental MSD data matching these key theoretical predictions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the rheological model, derives the governing Langevin equations for particle motion in the VE fluid, analyzes the resulting Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) across different timescale orderings ($	au_R$ vs $	au_k$ vs $\lambda$), and validates these theoretical predictions using both numerical simulations and physical experiments.
why_interesting: While focused on soft matter dynamics rather than quantum phenomena, the study of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics in complex fluids (like viscoelastic media) shares conceptual links with open quantum systems where environmental coupling dictates system evolution. The concept of tunable 'effective environments' is relevant to designing quantum simulators.
